newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil traders say rain won't slow soybean exports.
newsitem.headline: Brazil traders say rain won't slow soybean exports.

text.p: Brazilian soybean exports are unlikely to be affected by a delay in the harvest of early-cycle soybeans caused by heavy rains in the key growing state of Parana, traders said.
"I don't think (exports will be affected)," said one trader.

Traders pointed out that the harvest was progressing normally in Mato Grosso state, which is the main source of the early-cycle variety, and those areas affected in Parana had only planted a small amount of early-cycle soybeans.
"The amount coming out of Londrina shouldn't be that big," the trader said, referring to a region in Parana which has seen more than 250 mm of rain this month.
The Chicago market rose sharply on Tuesday on news of sharply higher-than-expected U.S. soybean export registrations and talk that heavy rains could delay exports of Brazilian soybeans.

Traders said the U.S. data, which showed that 35.2 million bushels were registered for export in the week ending Feb 13, had been the main factor driving the market although concerns about a delay in Brazil shipments may have boosted the figure.

"I think the rain may have had an effect on the U.S. export figures with people worrying there might be a delay out of Brazil and saying, 'Let's guarantee our supplies' and buying an extra shipment out of the U.S.," said one trader.
"It only takes a couple of firms to do that to drive the figure up," he said.
But he added: "I don't think that at the moment (the rain) is having too much effect."
Trade out of Brazil was sluggish as the market returned from last week's carnival holiday and enquiries were scarce.
One trader reported that 16,000 tonnes of soymeal had been sold for June/July shipment but did not specify the destination and price.

Brazil registered 2.35 million tonnes of soybeans from the 1997/98 harvest for export by Jan 30, according to Commerce Department figures published by independent consultants Safras e Mercado earlier this week.
This represented 40 percent of the total 5.8 million tonnes forecast to be exported this year, up from 34 percent at the same time last year, Safras said.
